text.p: Plans to merge Pacific Enterprises and Enova Corp are driven by growing competition in the natural gas and electricity industries, but some experts question who will actually benefit.
Los Angeles-based Pacific Enterprises is the parent of Southern California Gas Co, the largest U.S. gas distributor, while Enova is the parent of San Diego Gas & Electric Co.
"There is too much talk about the virtues of competition," said Gary Hovis an analyst at Argus Research. "There will be some cost savings, but don't expect much change for consumers."
San Francisco-based consumer advocates Toward Utility Rate Normalization (TURN) also questioned the merger's eventual benefit for customers.

"The good news is that this merger will create a big, aggressive competitor for Pacific Gas & Electric and Southern California Edison said Michael Florio, lead attorney for TURN. "The bad news is that it will also create a big, aggressive cross-subsidizer. SoCal Gas has been very aggressive in seeking to raise rates for its most-captive customers."

Florio also expressed concern about the potential diversion of utility revenues into an unregulated venture that Enova and Pacific plan to establish to pursue opportunities in the emerging market for energy services. In addition, TURN questioned if ratepayers would see much of the $1.2 billion in cost savings anticipated by the merger partners.
Others, including Hovis at Argus Research, said the estimate of $1.2 billion in savings over 10 years is "overblown" anyway.
"Based on past mergers, the actual savings will be a lot less than predicted," he said.
Some sources said the merger may offer more upside potential to Enova, while the benefits to Pacific Enterprises are less certain.
"The electric part is fine. It's a good deal for Enova," said another equity analyst. "They get a partner with a lot of money."
An executive at a Northwest utility said there is a risk on the San Diego side of losing customers once the state begins to phase-in competition in 1998.
"This deal puts San Diego in a pretty good position," he added.

SDG&E is already a net buyer of power and does not have the huge stranded costs that overhang the state's other two investor-owned utilities, Edison International's Southern California Edison Co and Pacific Gas and Electric.
Hovis also said merging the two utilities "will be good for all concerned in the long run," but Enova will benefit in the short-term by improving gas distribution.
"They already have the pipeline systems, there is no cost factor there," he noted.

Standard & Poor's on Tuesday said it revised the ratings outlook of San Diego Gas & Electric Co to positive from stable. But the rating firm revised its outlook for Pacific Enterprises and Southern California Gas Co to negative from stable.

S&P noted the ratings at both companies could be unchanged once the merger is complete, but operations may become more consolidated and the new company is likely to encounter greater business risk from utility deregulation and unbundling.
